title: Client-Server Model and APIs
description: Understand the fundamental pattern of how software communicates — clients ask, servers answer, and APIs define the language they speak.

segments.text: Every app on your phone, every website you visit — they all follow one fundamental pattern. Today we're going to understand that pattern from the ground up.
Meet the client. That's your browser, your mobile app, or any piece of software that needs something. Think of a client as a customer walking into a restaurant — they make requests.
And here's the server. It's a computer that listens for requests and sends back responses. Like the kitchen in our restaurant — it takes orders and prepares what was asked for.
The client sends a request: 'Give me the latest posts.' The server receives it, does the work, and sends back the data. This request-response cycle is the heartbeat of the entire web.
But here's the thing — the client and server need to speak the same language. If I walk into a restaurant and bark random words, the kitchen can't help me.
segments.thought_prompt: How do you think clients and servers agree on a shared 'language' for communication?

segments.text: That shared language is called an API — Application Programming Interface. It defines the endpoints: specific URLs that accept specific requests. Like a menu — it tells you exactly what you can order and how to order it.

REST is the most common API style. It uses HTTP methods you already know: GET to read data, POST to create, PUT to update, DELETE to remove. The URL identifies the resource — like /users/42 means 'user number 42'.

When the server responds, it typically sends back JSON — a simple format using curly braces, keys, and values. It's human-readable and machine-parseable. Think of it as a universal packaging format for data.

Every response includes a status code. 200 means success. 201 means created. 400 means you sent a bad request. 404 means not found. 500 means the server broke. These codes are your first debugging tool.

Here's a key insight: the client doesn't care HOW the server gets the answer. The server could use a database, call other services, or compute it on the fly. That separation is what makes the web so powerful.
segments.thought_prompt: Why is it useful that the client doesn't need to know what happens inside the server?

segments.text: Every major app works this way. When you scroll Instagram, the app sends GET requests. When you post a photo, that's a POST. When you delete a comment, that's a DELETE. APIs are everywhere.

So remember: clients request, servers respond, APIs define the contract between them, and JSON carries the data. This client-server model is the foundation everything else in system design builds upon.
